sentence: The one over many argument is the realist's central move: when many things are F, there is one thing, F-ness, that they all are. The nominalist denies the inference, holding that 'a and b are both F' need not commit us to an entity F-ness any more than 'a and b both exist' commits us to an entity, existence.

The special composition question asks under what conditions some things compose a further thing. Universalism says always, so there is an object composed of your nose and the moon. Nihilism says never, so strictly there are only simples arranged variously. The intuitive moderate answer, sometimes, has proven hard to state in a principled, non-arbitrary way.

subtopic: the self and the unity of consciousness
sentence: When I look within, I find perceptions, thoughts, and feelings, but I never seem to catch the self that is supposed to have them. Hume drew the radical conclusion that there is no such self, only a bundle of experiences. The unity we attribute to a mind would then be a construction, not a thing discovered, and the owner of experience would be a grammatical fiction.

The indispensability argument runs that we ought to believe in whatever our best science quantifies over, that science quantifies ineliminably over mathematical entities, and therefore that we ought to believe such entities exist. The nominalist must respond either by showing that mathematics can be eliminated from science or by denying that quantification carries ontological commitment.

Mary, raised in a black-and-white room, knows every physical fact about color vision. On her first sight of red, does she learn something new? If she does, then the physical facts were not all the facts, and phenomenal knowledge outruns physical knowledge. The physicalist must say either that she learns nothing, which seems false, or that she gains only a new ability, which relocates rather than removes the puzzle.

Temporal-parts theory offers a unified treatment. The statue and the lump are four-dimensional objects, and they overlap in some temporal parts while diverging in others. They are not two things wholly in one place; they are two space-time worms that share a temporal segment, the way two roads can share a stretch. The puzzles dissolve once persistence is reconceived as having parts in time.

Reliabilism shifts justification from the believer's reasons to the process that produced the belief: a belief is knowledge if formed by a process that reliably yields truths. This naturalizes knowledge and handles many cases. But the fake-barn case shows reliability must be local, and a process reliable in normal settings can fail to yield knowledge in a deceptive one.

subtopic: logic and the foundations of inference
sentence: Classical logic assumes bivalence, that every statement is true or false, and the law of excluded middle, that for any statement either it or its negation holds. Intuitionists reject excluded middle for statements we have no method to decide, holding that truth is not independent of provability. The disagreement is not merely technical; it reflects rival views of what truth is.

The difference principle holds that social and economic inequalities are just only if they work to the greatest advantage of the worst-off members of society. The thought is that natural talents are morally arbitrary, no one deserves their starting point, and so the distribution of talents should be treated as a common asset whose fruits are governed by terms fair to all.

Time, for the phenomenologist, is not first a sequence of instants but a lived flow with a thick present. Each now is fringed by a just-past that is still held, a retention, and a not-yet that is already anticipated, a protention. A melody is heard as a melody because the past notes are retained even as the present one sounds; without this structure there would be no experience of duration at all.

Phenomenology resists the demand to choose between idealism and realism as that demand is usually posed. It studies neither a mind sealed off from things nor things stripped of any relation to mind, but precisely the correlation between them, the way the world is given and the way subjectivity is open to it. Its subject matter is the meeting itself, prior to the abstractions that pull the two apart.

Aristotle locates each virtue as a mean between extremes: courage between cowardice and rashness, generosity between stinginess and prodigality. The mean is not a midpoint on a fixed scale but the response that fits the situation, the person, and the time. Hitting the mean is therefore a skill, sensitive to particulars, and not reducible to a formula that could be followed without perception.

Practical wisdom is the master virtue that coordinates the rest. Courage without wisdom becomes recklessness; generosity without wisdom becomes a soft touch. Wisdom is knowing what matters here and now, how the virtues bear on this case, and how to act when they seem to conflict. It is not a separate department of knowledge but the intelligence internal to virtue itself.

Some doubt that there is a single relation answering to the word 'cause.' Perhaps causation as conceived in fundamental physics, as understood in the special sciences, and as deployed in everyday explanation are distinct, only loosely related notions. If so, the search for the analysis of causation is misguided, and what is needed is a survey of a family of relations bound by family resemblance.

Reformed epistemology denies that religious belief needs the support of argument to be rational. Belief in God can be properly basic, formed directly in certain experiences much as perceptual beliefs are formed, and warranted if the cognitive faculty producing it is functioning well in a suitable environment. The dispute then shifts to whether there is such a faculty and how its reliability could be assessed.

The applicability of mathematics is itself a philosophical puzzle. Why should structures developed in abstraction turn out to describe the physical world so precisely, sometimes long before any application is found? The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics suggests either a deep harmony between thought and world, or that the world is, at bottom, mathematical, or that we are seeing a selection effect.

Inference to the best explanation is the realist's engine: we are entitled to believe the hypothesis that best explains the data. But what makes one explanation best, simplicity, scope, fertility, and why should those features track truth rather than merely our preferences? Unless explanatory virtue is connected to truth, the inference from best explanation to reality is left without a foundation.

To be authentic is to own one's existence, to acknowledge that one's life is one's own to make and that no role, custom, or authority can take the choosing off one's hands. Inauthenticity is the flight from this, the pretense that one merely follows what is done, that one's path was settled by circumstance. The existentialist holds that even the refusal to choose is itself a choice.

Perceptual experience seems to outrun the concepts the perceiver possesses. I can see a shade of red far more specific than any color concept I have, and discriminate it without being able to name or re-identify it. This suggests perceptual content is, at least in part, non-conceptual, finer-grained than thought, which would mean the senses give us more than the understanding can take up.

Functionalism proposes that mental states are defined by their causal roles, not by their substrate: pain is whatever is typically caused by injury and typically causes avoidance, whether realized in neurons or silicon. This explains how the same mental state could occur in very different physical systems. Its limit is the felt quality of experience, which seems to outrun any specification of role.

The disagreement of an acknowledged epistemic peer poses a sharp challenge. If someone equally informed and equally careful reaches the opposite conclusion, conciliationism says you should reduce your confidence, perhaps splitting the difference. Steadfast views say you may rationally retain your view, since you have your reasons. How much another's dissent should move us is unresolved and consequential.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: Coherentists can answer the isolation objection by building observational constraints into coherence: a maximally coherent system must accommodate the spontaneous beliefs that perception forces on us. The web is then not free-floating but anchored by inputs it cannot simply ignore. Whether this concedes a kind of foundation, in the privileged status of observation, is a question coherentists must face.

There is a question whether epistemic justification aims solely at truth or also serves other ends. If the goal is truth, then justified believing is believing in a way conducive to getting things right. But understanding, coherence, and explanatory depth seem to be epistemic goods too, and they do not reduce neatly to truth-conduciveness, suggesting the aims of inquiry are plural.

subtopic: the limits of language and the unsayable
sentence: The relation between a name and the world it touches has a quality that is hard to put into further words. We can say that 'snow' refers to snow, but the saying uses the very relation it is trying to describe. There may be a sense in which the bond between language and reality can be exhibited only in the using and not surveyed from outside.

subtopic: power, ideology, and the critique of reason
sentence: Ideology can operate not by stating falsehoods but by what it leaves unsaid, by framing a question so that certain options never come into view. The most effective constraint may be on the imagination, on the sense of what is possible. To criticize ideology is then partly to expand the field of the thinkable, to make visible the alternatives a settled common sense has hidden.

Indexicals like 'I,' 'here,' and 'now' refer in a way no name or description matches. 'I' refers to whoever utters it, automatically and without descriptive backing. The thought I express with 'I am in danger' cannot be fully captured by any third-person description, which suggests there is an irreducibly first-personal mode of reference and of belief.

Nozick objected that a just distribution cannot be specified by any end-state pattern. Justice is historical: a holding is just if justly acquired and justly transferred, whatever overall pattern results. Liberty upsets patterns, since free exchanges by people entitled to their holdings will produce inequalities, and to maintain a favored pattern would require continual interference with voluntary transactions.

The design argument infers a designer from the apparent fine-tuning of the cosmos and the intricate adaptation of living things. Critics reply that evolution explains biological adaptation without design, and that fine-tuning may be an artifact of observer selection, since only a life-permitting universe could be observed at all. The argument's force depends on whether such alternatives are genuinely available.

Kripke's causal-historical picture proposes that a name refers in virtue of a chain reaching back from current use to an initial baptism of the object. Speakers down the chain need know almost nothing true of the referent; they borrow the reference from those they learned the name from. Reference becomes a social and historical relation, not a private cognitive achievement.

If understanding is always shaped by the interpreter's situation, the worry arises that interpretation is merely the projection of present concerns onto the past. The hermeneutic reply is that genuine interpretation is a conversation in which the text retains the power to surprise and resist. An interpretation that only confirmed the interpreter's prior views would, by that very fact, not be an interpretation at all.

Frankfurt cases challenge the link between responsibility and the ability to do otherwise. Imagine a device that would intervene to force a choice, but only if the agent showed signs of choosing differently. The agent chooses freely, the device never acts, and yet the agent could not have done otherwise. If we still hold the agent responsible, then alternative possibilities are not what responsibility requires.

Rights of future persons present a puzzle. People not yet born can be harmed by what we do, yet they do not now exist to bear claims, and which individuals will exist depends on our choices. If a polluting policy changes who is born, the future people it harms would not have existed under a cleaner policy, complicating the claim that they were wronged.

Gödel showed that any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic contains truths it cannot prove. This has been read as evidence that mathematical truth outruns provability, and so supports a platonism on which truth is independent of our methods. Others resist the philosophical reading, holding that the theorem is a technical result about formal systems and settles no metaphysical question.

Whether perception is cognitively penetrable, shaped by belief, expectation, and desire, bears on its role as evidence. If what we see is partly determined by what we already think, then perception cannot serve as a neutral check on theory, since theory would have colored the perception in advance. The extent of such penetration is an empirical and philosophical battleground.

The experimental critique notes that intuitions vary with the order in which cases are presented, with the wording, with the cultural background of the respondent, and with factors that ought to be morally irrelevant. If our verdicts about imagined cases are this unstable, their evidential value is in doubt, and a method built on them may be building on shifting ground.

One may hold that the proper relation of faith and reason is neither dominance nor divorce but a kind of mutual correction. Reason can examine the coherence of religious concepts and the cogency of arguments; faith can press questions, such as the meaning of suffering, that argument alone leaves cold. Whether this division is stable, or collapses toward one side, is itself a long-running question.

Permissivism holds that a single body of evidence can rationally support more than one doxastic attitude, so that two equally rational agents with the same evidence might believe differently. Uniqueness denies this, holding that evidence determines exactly one rational response. The dispute bears on whether rationality leaves room for legitimate intellectual individuality or demands convergence.

A subtler worry concerns what well-being is. If it is pleasure, the experience machine threatens the theory, since plugging everyone into blissful illusion would maximize pleasure yet seems a failure. If it is preference satisfaction, malformed or malicious preferences count. If it is an objective list, the theory must defend the list. The aggregation problem presupposes a currency, and the choice of currency is itself contested.

Justice between generations and across borders strains theories built for a single society. If the principles are addressed to those who cooperate within shared institutions, what do they say about people in distant nations or in the future, with whom one shares no such institutions? Either justice extends beyond cooperative schemes, or much of the world falls outside its reach.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: Yet the cases earn their keep precisely by being controlled experiments. By varying one feature at a time, they isolate which features our moral judgment is sensitive to. The artificiality is the point: it strips away confounds. The question is not whether the scenarios are realistic but whether the factors they isolate are morally relevant, and that is a question intuition cannot settle by itself.

Emotions may be sources of practical knowledge, not obstacles to it. Compassion can disclose the reality of another's suffering in a way detached calculation misses; indignation can register an injustice before any argument articulates it. On this view, the well-functioning emotions are a faculty of moral perception, and a person of pure intellect, feeling nothing, would not see clearly but would be morally blind.

The puzzle sharpens when we ask about responsibility. If the person who committed an act long ago is connected to the present person only by an attenuated psychological chain, in what sense is the present person the same one who acted? Our practices of praise and blame assume an identity robust enough to bear moral weight, yet the metaphysics struggles to supply anything that robust.

Against modal realism stands the incredulous stare: it is hard to believe there really exist talking donkeys and blue swans, just elsewhere. The realist replies that the stare is not an argument and that the benefits in theory outweigh the affront to common sense. The dispute exposes how much weight intuitions about existence should carry against systematic gains.

Subjectivism says a life means whatever its liver takes it to mean: meaning is constituted by being gripped, by caring deeply about one's pursuits. But this seems to let too much in. A life consumed by counting blades of grass would be meaningful if the counter were sufficiently absorbed, and most resist that verdict, which suggests meaning answers to standards beyond mere absorption.

Objectivism replies that some pursuits are more worthy of devotion than others, and a life is meaningful when subjective engagement attaches to objectively worthwhile ends. The hybrid slogan is that meaning arises where subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness. The unresolved task is to ground the objective side without an appeal to authority that naturalism cannot supply.

The naturalist locates meaning in features available within a finite, godless life: love, achievement, understanding, the alleviation of suffering. On this view a life is meaningful insofar as it is actively engaged with things of genuine worth. The challenge is to say which things have genuine worth without smuggling back the cosmic guarantee that naturalism set aside.

Every inference from observed regularities to unobserved cases assumes that the future will resemble the past. But that assumption cannot be established by experience without circularity, since any such argument would itself rely on induction. Nor can it be a truth of logic, since a chaotic future is not contradictory. So our most basic mode of empirical reasoning rests on a premise we can neither prove nor do without.

Utilitarianism holds that the right act is the one that produces the greatest total well-being. Its appeal is its impartiality: each person's good counts once, no more and no less. But this impartiality is also its difficulty, for it permits, and sometimes requires, sacrificing one person's vital interests whenever doing so yields a larger sum elsewhere. The theory treats persons as locations of value rather than as separate sources of claims.

The phenomenal character of perception, the felt quality of seeing red or hearing a tone, may or may not be exhausted by representational content. If two experiences could represent exactly the same and yet feel different, then perception has a qualitative dimension beyond its content. If not, then to capture how an experience is, in itself, is just to capture how it presents the world to be.

Kant grounds constraints in the categorical imperative: act only on a maxim you could will as universal law. A maxim of lying for advantage cannot be universalized, since universal lying would destroy the trust that lying exploits. The constraint against lying is thus not a brute prohibition but a requirement of consistency in willing, derived from the bare idea of acting on principle.

A subtler relativism is agent-relativism, the claim that an act can be right relative to one moral framework and wrong relative to another, with no framework-independent fact settling the matter. The challenge for this view is to explain the practice of moral argument, in which we treat ourselves as disagreeing rather than merely as occupying different frameworks that cannot, in principle, conflict.

The easy problems concern mechanisms: how attention selects, how memory consolidates, how a system reports its own states. These yield to ordinary scientific methods. The hard problem is different in kind, because solving every easy problem would still leave the question of experience open. That asymmetry suggests the hard problem is not merely harder but structurally resistant to the explanatory style that works elsewhere.

Concern for others may not be a single thing. There is the cool recognition that another's claim is valid, the warm sympathy that feels their distress, and the identification that makes their good one's own. These can come apart: one can recognize a duty without feeling sympathy, or feel sympathy without acknowledging a claim. A theory of moral motivation must map this terrain rather than reduce it to one item.

There is a worry that relentless self-examination can corrode the spontaneity that a good life also seems to need. The person forever standing outside their own actions to assess them may lose the capacity to be simply absorbed in living. If so, wisdom is not maximal reflection but the right rhythm of reflection and engagement, knowing when to question and when to act.

Does perception have content, a way it represents the world as being, that can be accurate or inaccurate? The representationalist says yes: an experience is like a belief in presenting the world thus-and-so. The relationalist says perception is more basic, a direct acquaintance with objects and their properties, not a representing of them. The dispute concerns whether experience is fundamentally a depicting or a presenting.

If emotions can be reasonable or unreasonable, then there is such a thing as emotional rationality, a fittingness of feeling to circumstance. To feel grief at a loss is fitting; to feel it at a trifle is not. This suggests a normative dimension of the emotional life parallel to the normative dimension of belief, with its own standards of getting things right.

Bad faith is self-deception about one's own freedom. The waiter who plays at being a waiter, the person who insists they simply are what their situation made them, both disown the freedom they are exercising in that very disowning. Bad faith is possible because a person is at once a free project and a being with a given situation, and bad faith collapses one of these into the other.

The acquaintance principle holds that aesthetic judgments must be made first-hand: one cannot know a poem is beautiful on testimony, as one can know a fact. If true, this marks aesthetic value as essentially tied to experience, not a fact one could simply be told. The defender of testimony replies that we do, in practice, defer to critics, and that aesthetic knowledge is not so isolated.

The puzzle of empty names is sharp. 'Vulcan does not exist' seems true and meaningful, yet if a name's whole job is to refer, an empty name should be meaningless and the sentence should fail to say anything. Either names contribute something beyond a referent, or sentences with empty names are not what they appear, perhaps disguised quantifications.

The disjunction problem haunts every naturalistic theory of content. Whatever you say a state is reliably caused by, there is a disjunctive alternative it is also caused by, and nothing in the causal facts privileges the non-disjunctive reading. Until a principled way is found to break such ties, the determinacy of what we think will lack a naturalistic explanation.

The will theory holds instead that a right is a protected sphere of choice: to have a right is to have control over another's duty, the power to demand performance or to waive it. This explains rights that license self-harming choices. But it struggles to attribute rights to those who cannot exercise choice, such as infants or the severely incapacitated, whom we nonetheless think have rights.

Truth is plausibly bivalent for ordinary claims, yet vague and future-contingent statements strain bivalence. Is it now true that a borderline-bald man is bald, or that there will be a sea battle tomorrow? If every meaningful claim is determinately true or false, vagueness and the open future become deeply puzzling; if not, classical logic must be revised.

Some moral judgments seem to resist relativization no matter how the cultural facts run. The wrongness of torturing children for amusement does not feel like something that could be true here and false elsewhere. If even one moral claim is objectively true, full relativism is false, and the relativist must either deny the appearance or explain it away as mere strength of feeling.

If the external world is a hypothesis inferred from experience, the inference must be ampliative, and so it inherits all the difficulties of ampliative reasoning. The realist replies that the external world is not inferred at all but is the framework within which inference takes place. Whether that reply is a solution or a refusal to play the skeptic's game is itself a hard question.

subtopic: the categorical imperative and moral law
sentence: Consider the maxim of making a false promise to escape a difficulty. Universalized, promising would lose its function, since no one would credit a promise; the maxim, made universal, undermines the very practice it exploits. This is a contradiction in conception, and it shows, on Kant's account, that false promising is wrong not by its results but by its incoherence as a principle.

To ask for the meaning of life is to ask an oddly framed question, since meaning is usually a relation between a sign and what it stands for, and a life is not a sign. Perhaps the real question is whether a life can matter, whether it can be worth living from the inside and worth something beyond itself. Reframed this way, the question loses its mystical air and becomes tractable, though no easier to answer.

Some hold that truth is one thing in mathematics and another in ethics or comedy, so that what makes a moral claim true differs from what makes an arithmetical claim true. This pluralism accommodates the diversity of discourse. Its difficulty is to explain how a single inference can move validly across domains, mixing premises whose truth would, on this view, be different properties.

There is a tension between thinking death bad and thinking one's own death not to be feared. One might hold both: death is a real misfortune, depriving us of goods, yet fearing it changes nothing and corrodes the present. Wisdom might consist in acknowledging the loss clearly while declining to let the anticipation of it darken the time one has.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: A response distinguishes the having of a reason from the giving of one. Perhaps a belief can be properly basic if it is formed in the right circumstances by the right faculty, without the believer needing a further belief that the circumstances and faculty are reliable. Justification then becomes a feature of belief formation rather than of a chain of arguments the believer can produce.

subtopic: logic and the foundations of inference
sentence: What justifies a basic rule of inference such as modus ponens? Any argument for it would seem to use inference, and probably modus ponens itself, making the justification circular. This is a regress problem for logic. One response holds that the most basic rules are not justified by anything more basic but are constitutive of reasoning, so that to demand a justification for them is to misunderstand their role.

subtopic: logic and the foundations of inference
sentence: The paradoxes of material implication are a standing irritant. In classical logic, a false statement implies anything, and a true statement is implied by anything, so 'if the moon is cheese then 2+2=4' counts as true. Relevant logics try to restore a connection of relevance between antecedent and consequent, holding that genuine implication requires more than a truth-functional accident.

If free will is an illusion, our reactive attitudes of resentment and gratitude rest on a mistake. Yet a strict eliminativism about these attitudes may be psychologically impossible and socially corrosive. Some argue we should retain the practices while revising their justification, grounding blame in its forward-looking effects rather than in backward-looking desert.

Logicism aimed to show that mathematics is reducible to logic, that arithmetical truths are logical truths in disguise and arithmetical objects definable in purely logical terms. The program ran into the paradoxes of naive set theory and the need for axioms, such as infinity, that do not look like truths of logic. Whether any descendant of logicism can succeed remains an open question.

Consider whether tiny benefits to many can outweigh a great harm to one. If a billion people each gain a trivial pleasure, may we justly impose torture on a single innocent? The utilitarian arithmetic says yes if the sum is large enough. Many find this monstrous, and the example pressures whether welfare is the kind of thing that can be summed without limit across persons at all.

Emotions seem to involve the body in a way pure thought does not: the racing heart of fear, the heat of anger, the heaviness of grief. One tradition holds the bodily disturbance is the emotion; another holds it is a mere accompaniment. The truth may be that emotion is neither pure cognition nor pure feeling but an integrated response in which appraisal, feeling, and bodily change are aspects of one thing.

Wisdom may consist partly in knowing which questions to leave open. Not every problem can be solved, and a person who insists on certainty where none is available, or who treats every uncertainty as intolerable, lacks something. Part of living well, on this view, is a trained capacity to act and to be at peace amid questions that remain, honestly, unsettled.

The marginal cases argument presses that whatever cognitive capacity is proposed as the ground of full human status, some humans, infants or the severely cognitively impaired, will lack it, while some animals possess it. If we still accord those humans full status, we cannot consistently deny status to animals with equal or greater capacities, on pain of arbitrariness.

subtopic: power, ideology, and the critique of reason
sentence: Critical theory holds that a satisfactory social theory is not merely descriptive but emancipatory: it should be informed by an interest in freeing people from unnecessary forms of domination. This makes the theory itself a practical undertaking, answerable not only to truth but to whether it can illuminate and help dissolve the constraints it studies.

The access problem is the central challenge to mathematical platonism. Knowledge usually involves some causal contact between knower and known, but abstract objects, by definition, cause nothing. If our mathematical beliefs are not connected to mathematical reality by any reliable mechanism, it becomes a mystery how those beliefs could amount to knowledge rather than lucky guesses.

The relativist sometimes argues from the difficulty of proving moral claims. But difficulty of proof is not absence of truth; many objective matters are hard to settle. And the relativist's own thesis, that all morality is relative, is itself a hard-to-prove general claim, so the appeal to unprovability, if it works, works against relativism as much as against its rival.

Preemption is the hardest case. Two assassins, one fires first and kills the victim; the second would have killed him had the first not fired. The first shot caused the death, yet had it not occurred, the death would still have happened, courtesy of the backup. The simple counterfactual gives the wrong verdict, and repairing it without ad hoc patching is notoriously difficult.

Descartes held that animals are mere automata, machines without consciousness, their cries no more than the creaking of mechanism. The view has few defenders now, but the underlying problem persists: we cannot directly observe another creature's experience, and the inference to animal consciousness rests on behavioral and physiological analogy, which the skeptic can always question.

If aesthetic value is real, it raises a question of normativity: does beauty give us reason to attend, to preserve, to create? An object's being beautiful seems to make a claim on us, calling for a certain response. Whether that claim is as binding as a moral one, and how an aesthetic reason competes with reasons of other kinds, is a question aesthetics shares with ethics.

The world appears as a meaningful whole before it is parsed into discrete facts. A room is encountered as inviting or oppressive, a tool as ready-to-hand for a task, a path as walkable. The phenomenologist argues that this practical, holistic appearing is primary, and that the detached survey of bare objects with properties is a later, derivative attitude, not the foundation of experience.

subtopic: the categorical imperative and moral law
sentence: Kant claims the several formulations of the categorical imperative are equivalent, each expressing the same principle from a different side. The universal-law formula stresses the form of a moral maxim; the humanity formula its matter, the ends it must respect; the kingdom-of-ends formula the systematic whole of agents legislating together. Whether they truly coincide in their verdicts has been much disputed.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: Infinitism accepts the regress and embraces an actual infinity of reasons, each justified by the next. The view is logically possible but psychologically strained, since finite minds cannot survey infinite chains. Defenders reply that justification can be a matter of reasons being available, not actually entertained, but critics doubt that an availability never cashed out confers genuine warrant.

subtopic: political authority and the social contract
sentence: Hobbes pictured a state of nature without common power as a war of all against all, where life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. Rational individuals, to escape it, would covenant to surrender their right of self-rule to a sovereign. Authority is justified because any settled order is better than the terror of having none, and the contract is an inference from what reason would dictate.

subtopic: the self and the unity of consciousness
sentence: There is a distinction between the self as subject and the self as object. The self as object is the empirical person, with a body and a biography, available to be studied. The self as subject is the standpoint from which anything is experienced at all, and it seems to recede whenever one tries to make it an object, since any object is something the subject is over against.

The deductivist hope is to recast science so that it never infers inductively, only conjectures boldly and refutes by deduction. But even severe testing leaves us with a theory not yet refuted, and the decision to rely on such a theory for prediction is itself an inductive leap. Banishing induction from the logic of discovery does not banish it from the logic of action.

Yet emotions can also distort. They are partial, attached to the near and the vivid, swayed by how things are framed. A theory that honors their cognitive role must also acknowledge their unreliability, and the result is that emotions, like the senses, are evidence to be weighed and educated rather than either trusted absolutely or dismissed.

Perhaps the dispute is partly verbal. Both sides agree on the facts: the world may be deterministic, agents deliberate, deliberation causes action, and some agents are coerced while others are not. They disagree about which package of facts deserves the honorific 'free.' If so, the substantive questions concern responsibility and control, and the word 'free' is a label whose attachment is the last and least important step.

Epicurus argued that death is nothing to us: while we exist, death is not present, and when death is present, we do not exist; so it can never be experienced by anyone. If harm requires a subject to suffer it, and death removes the subject, then death harms no one. The argument is simple, ancient, and yet most find it impossible fully to believe.

Definite descriptions, on Russell's analysis, are not referring expressions at all. 'The king of France is bald' asserts that there is exactly one king of France and that he is bald, so the sentence is simply false when there is no such king, rather than failing to express a proposition. The analysis dissolves a puzzle by denying that 'the king of France' picks anything out.

A standing question is whether virtue ethics needs supplementing by an account of which traits are virtues. To say a virtue is a trait that contributes to flourishing presupposes a conception of flourishing, and that conception is itself ethically loaded. Without an independent grip on the human good, the theory risks circularity: virtues are what the flourishing life contains, and the flourishing life is the one lived virtuously.

Laws of nature stand at the center of scientific explanation, yet their own status is unclear. Are they mere regularities, descriptions of how things happen to go, or do they govern, supporting counterfactuals and constraining the possible? If laws are just regularities, it is hard to see why they explain; if they govern, one must say what kind of necessity a law carries and where it comes from.

Evolutionary debunking arguments contend that our moral beliefs were shaped by selection pressures aimed at survival, not at tracking moral truth, so even if such truths exist, our access to them would be a lucky accident. The realist must show that the forces that gave us moral capacities are not wholly off-track, perhaps because tracking certain genuine values was itself adaptive.

Eliminativists about content suggest that the very idea of states with determinate aboutness belongs to a folk theory that mature science will discard, as it discarded the humors. If there are no contents, the puzzle of how matter could have them dissolves. But the proposal seems self-undermining, since to assert it is to express a contentful claim, and to argue for it is to deploy contents in inference.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: One might reject the regress argument's framing. Perhaps justification is not always a matter of having reasons one can articulate. A belief may be justified because it is the default until challenged, with the burden falling on the doubter rather than the believer. This shifts the regress: not every belief needs a positive credential, only those that have come under specific suspicion.

The natural attitude takes the existence of the world for granted and asks only about the things within it. The phenomenological reduction suspends that assumption, not to doubt the world but to make visible the achievement by which a world is constituted for consciousness. What was a silent background becomes a theme, and the constituting of sense becomes available for description.

The realist about ontology resists deflation. There is, the realist holds, a fact about what the world fundamentally contains, and getting it right is a substantive achievement, not a choice of idiom. The dispute about composition, whether arrangements of simples ever compose a further thing, is then a real dispute with a real answer, even if it is hard to discover.

Fictionalism holds that mathematical statements are, strictly, false, since there are no numbers, but that the practice of mathematics is nonetheless valuable, a useful fiction whose value lies in its applications and inferential structure. Engaging in mathematics is then like engaging with a story. The objection is that mathematics does not feel like fiction; its claims feel forced upon us, not invented.

subtopic: the is-ought problem and the grounds of value
sentence: If oughts cannot be derived from facts, perhaps they are not derived at all but expressed. The non-cognitivist holds that to reach an evaluative conclusion is to take up an attitude, not to infer a further fact, and so there is no missing premise, because the conclusion was never a factual claim. The is-ought gap is then not a gap in inference but a difference in the kind of speech act.

Sensitivity analyses say you know that p only if, were p false, you would not believe it. This elegantly explains why you do not know you are not a brain in a vat, since if you were, you would still believe you were not. But it also seems to deny obvious knowledge, and it can fail to be closed under known entailment, which strikes many as a defect.

Existence precedes essence: a human being is not made to a prior specification, the way a tool is made for its function, but first exists and only then defines what it will be through its choices. There is no human nature laid down in advance to which one must conform. This is the source of both the freedom and the burden the existentialist places at the center of a life.

The fission case is decisive against simple psychological criteria. If your brain were divided and each half placed in a new body, both successors would stand in the relation that supposedly constitutes identity. They cannot both be you, since they are not each other. So either identity is not what matters in survival, or the criterion is wrong, and the more honest conclusion may be the former.

The existentialist denies that freedom is comfortable. To be free is to be condemned to choose, to be unable to lean on a given nature or an external command to do the choosing for us. Every excuse that points beyond the self, to circumstance or to expectation, is, on this account, a way of pretending that the burden of freedom can be set down, which it cannot.

The demandingness objection notes that if I must always maximize total welfare, then every dollar spent on myself beyond bare subsistence is a dollar withheld from those in greater need. The theory leaves no space for personal projects, no moral room of one's own. Either morality really is this demanding, or a credible theory must make room for prerogatives, and utilitarianism in its pure form makes none.

Some emotions seem to have intrinsic value, to be part of a life worth living rather than mere means to it. Love, joy, and grief are not just instruments; a life without them would be impoverished even if it were otherwise pleasant. If this is right, then a purely instrumental view of emotion, treating feelings only by their effects, misses much of what makes them matter.

Disagreement in taste need not show that there is nothing to be right about. Two people may diverge because one has not noticed a feature the other has, or lacks the training to perceive it. On this view aesthetic disagreement is often resolvable in principle by more attentive looking, and the relativist's appeal to brute difference of taste underestimates how much aesthetic perception can be improved.

The supernaturalist holds that a life has meaning only if it plays a role in a larger divine plan. The worry is that being a part in someone else's purpose, however grand, does not obviously confer meaning; a cog serves the machine without its life thereby meaning anything. If meaning requires that one's own purposes count, an external plan may be neither necessary nor sufficient.

Are emotions opposed to reason, intrusions of feeling that cloud judgment, or are they themselves a form of judgment? The cognitive theory of emotion holds that an emotion involves an evaluative appraisal: fear is, in part, the judgment that something is dangerous, anger the judgment that one has been wronged. On this view emotions can be assessed as apt or inapt, reasonable or unreasonable, like beliefs.

To deny the hard problem outright is to claim that once the functional and informational facts are settled, there is simply no further fact about experience. This eliminativist move is consistent, but it asks us to treat the most certain thing we know, that we are conscious, as a confusion. The strangeness of that demand is itself evidence that the problem is not so easily waved away.

Mathematical truths seem necessary: it is not merely a fact that seven is prime, but a fact that could not have been otherwise. Explaining this necessity is a constraint on any philosophy of mathematics. Platonism locates it in the eternal nature of abstract objects; conventionalism in our rules; neither account has won general assent, and the modal status of mathematics remains contested.

subtopic: the is-ought problem and the grounds of value
sentence: Constructivists locate the grounds of value not in the world of facts and not in mere attitude but in the standpoint of practical reason itself. Oughts are derived not from is-statements but from what any rational agent, simply in deliberating, is committed to. The is-ought gap is respected, since the conclusions flow from the structure of agency, not from descriptive premises.

subtopic: the is-ought problem and the grounds of value
sentence: The naturalistic fallacy, as it is often called, charges that to define a moral term by a natural one, to say that good just means pleasant, or desired, or fitness-promoting, is to commit an error. For any natural property proposed, it remains an open, non-trivial question whether what has it is good, and that openness suggests good is not identical with the natural property.

The deepest worry is not about doing otherwise but about ultimate origination. To be truly responsible for an action, one would have to be responsible for the desires and character from which it flowed; but those were shaped by earlier factors one did not choose, regressing to factors before one's birth. This regress suggests that ultimate self-creation is impossible, and with it a certain absolute notion of desert.

Expressivism holds that moral statements do not describe facts but express attitudes: to say cruelty is wrong is to voice disapproval, not to report a property. This neatly explains the intimate link between moral judgment and motivation, since attitudes move us as beliefs alone may not. But it must then explain how moral sentences embed in conditionals and arguments, where they seem to behave exactly like ordinary truth-apt claims.

Frege distinguished sense from reference to explain how 'the morning star is the evening star' can be informative though both terms name Venus. The terms share a reference but differ in sense, in mode of presentation. Sense also explains how a name can be meaningful when its bearer does not exist. Whether genuine names have sense, or only reference, remains disputed.

The argument from illusion runs that since a straight stick can look bent in water, what one is directly aware of is something bent, and since the stick is not bent, that something is not the stick. Generalized, the argument concludes we are never directly aware of physical objects. Its weak point is the move from 'looks bent' to 'one is aware of something bent.'

Presentism says only the present exists; the past has ceased and the future is not yet. This matches the intuitive thought that what is over is gone. But it must explain how claims about the past can be true if there is nothing for them to be true of, and how present things can stand in relations to non-existent past ones.

Constraints generate the paradox of deontology: if violating a constraint once would prevent five future violations of the same constraint, the deontologist forbids the violation, thereby allowing more constraint-breaking overall. This looks irrational if constraints express the badness of the act-type. The deontologist must hold that constraints are agent-relative directives, not impersonal goals, and defend that conception of moral structure.

Phenomenology begins by attending to experience as it is lived, before theory tells us what it must be. The instruction is to describe rather than explain: to set aside, for a moment, the question whether what appears is real, and simply attend to the structure of the appearing itself. This bracketing is not denial but a discipline of looking, and it discloses features ordinary attitudes pass over.

Higher-order evidence raises a puzzle. Suppose you reason carefully to a conclusion, then learn that a drug has impaired reasoners like you. Your first-order evidence still supports the conclusion, but you now have evidence that your assessment of it may be flawed. Whether and how this should move you, and how to weigh evidence about evidence, is a question that ordinary accounts of justification did not anticipate.

Some necessities seem to hold not by logic but by the nature of things: water is necessarily H2O, gold necessarily has its atomic number. These metaphysical necessities are discovered empirically yet hold in every possible world. They suggest that the space of possible worlds is shaped by the essences of natural kinds, not merely by what is logically consistent.

Evidentialism holds that the justification of a belief is fixed entirely by the evidence the believer possesses: one is justified in believing exactly what one's evidence supports. This is elegant, but it must say what evidence is, how possession of evidence is determined, and what the support relation amounts to. Each of these has proven to harbor its own difficulties.

There is a question whether philosophy could proceed without intuitions at all. Even the arguments meant to discredit intuition seem to rest, somewhere, on judgments that strike the philosopher as compelling without further proof. If intuition cannot be wholly eliminated, the realistic project is to discipline it, not to dispense with it, and to be explicit about where and how it is being relied upon.

subtopic: foundationalism and the regress of justification
sentence: The regress problem may be less a problem to be solved than a map of the options for the structure of justification. Each escape route, foundations, webs, infinite chains, or default entitlement, encodes a different picture of what it is for a belief to be in good standing, and choosing among them is choosing a conception of epistemic order itself.

Deontology holds that certain acts are forbidden whatever the consequences: do not kill the innocent, do not lie, do not break faith. The hard case is the threshold: if keeping a constraint will cost a thousand lives, does it still bind? An absolutist says yes, which can seem fanatical; a moderate allows the constraint to be overridden, which can seem to concede that consequences govern after all. The challenge is to occupy a coherent middle.

Other people are not given to me as I give myself other objects. I do not infer a mind behind the moving body; I perceive the other directly as a perceiving subject, as another center of a world. This experience of the other poses a puzzle: how can a foreign subjectivity, by definition not mine, be present to me at all, and yet phenomenology insists that it is.

Against soul-making, one may press the case of suffering that breaks rather than builds, that destroys the sufferer before any soul could be made, or that falls on those, such as infants and animals, incapable of moral development. If suffering is justified by the growth it permits, suffering that permits no growth is left unexplained, and there is a great deal of it.

The charge of speciesism holds that giving lesser weight to a being's interests merely because it belongs to another species is a prejudice structurally like racism, an arbitrary partiality toward one's own kind. Defenders of a moral difference between humans and animals must then identify a morally relevant property that humans have and animals lack, and not merely point to species membership.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: Some argue the relevant factor is agency versus patiency: pushing treats the man as a mere object to be deployed, while diverting redirects an existing threat. To use a person is to fail to respect his separateness, regardless of outcomes. This Kantian thought explains the asymmetry without appeal to intention, by appeal instead to the kind of treatment a person is owed.

subtopic: power, ideology, and the critique of reason
sentence: Standpoint theory argues that social position affects what one can know, and that the perspective of the dominated can be epistemically privileged, since those who must navigate a system from below often see workings of it that are invisible from above. The claim is not that the marginalized are automatically right but that their vantage discloses what a dominant perspective is structured to overlook.

Modal skeptics suspect the whole apparatus answers a pseudo-question. They grant that we make modal claims and reason with them but deny that this commits us to an exotic plurality of worlds. On a deflationary view, to say something is possible is to say no more than that it is, in some sense, allowed; positing worlds to back this is to reify a façon de parler.

subtopic: determinism, chance, and the open future
sentence: Determinism is the thesis that the state of the world at any time, together with the laws, fixes the state at every other time. It is a claim about the world, not about predictability; a deterministic world might be unpredictable to any finite mind. Conversely, an indeterministic world might happen to be predictable on average. The two notions, often run together, are distinct.

Posthumous harms test our notion of welfare. If a person's deepest projects are betrayed after they die, are they thereby harmed, though they will never know? If the answer is yes, welfare extends beyond experience and beyond life; if no, then the value of a life is sealed at its end, and what happens after cannot touch it.

subtopic: the limits of language and the unsayable
sentence: Ordinary language is shot through with vagueness, metaphor, and indeterminacy, and the dream of a perfectly precise language, in which every term has sharp boundaries, has repeatedly failed. Perhaps this is not a defect to be cured. The flexibility of language may be exactly what allows it to track a world that does not come pre-divided into sharp kinds.

Philosophy relies heavily on imagined cases: a person split in two, a runaway trolley, a machine that delivers any experience. We consult our reactions to these scenarios and treat the reactions as evidence. But it is far from obvious why a feeling about a fictional case should tell us anything about the nature of personal identity, of right action, or of well-being.

Universals would explain not only shared character but also the lawlike connections between properties. If laws are relations among universals, then it being a law that all F are G is a fact about F-ness and G-ness themselves. Nominalists owe an account of natural law that does not quantify over such repeatable entities, and giving one has proven hard.

In the end, philosophy may not so much answer the question of how to live as keep it open and alive. Its value would then lie less in a doctrine handed over than in a sustained refusal to let the question be smothered by habit, by authority, or by the demands of getting through the day. The examined life is one in which that question is never finally allowed to fall silent.

Bizarre cases are sometimes dismissed as too far from ordinary life to teach us anything. But the strangeness can be the virtue. By taking a factor to an extreme, a far-fetched scenario can reveal whether a principle truly holds or merely seemed to, and a theory that gives a monstrous verdict in an outlandish case has told us something, even if what it has told us is hard to interpret.

Naturalist realism identifies moral facts with natural facts: perhaps rightness is what promotes well-being, and well-being is itself a natural condition. This makes moral knowledge continuous with empirical inquiry. The open-question argument objects that for any natural property proposed, it remains a substantive question whether what has it is good, suggesting goodness is not identical to any natural property after all.

Relative identity holds that there is no such thing as being simply the same, only being the same F. Two things can be the same lump and yet not the same statue. This dissolves the statue puzzle elegantly, but it abandons the classical notion of identity, and many find that too high a price, since the idea of a thing's being absolutely identical with itself seems indispensable.

The amoralist tests the internalist thesis. Imagine someone who uses moral words competently, agrees that cruelty is wrong, yet is wholly unmoved. If such a person is genuinely possible, moral judgment does not entail motivation. If the amoralist is only feigning the judgment, or using moral words in an inverted-commas sense, internalism survives. The case turns on what counts as a genuine moral judgment.

The open future raises the question whether statements about contingent future events are now true. If 'there will be a sea battle tomorrow' is already true, the future seems fixed; if already false, equally so. To preserve openness, one might deny present truth-value to such statements, but that requires departing from classical bivalence.

Anxiety, for the existentialist, is not fear of any particular thing but the dizziness of freedom: the recognition that nothing fixes what I will do, that the future is mine to determine and that no railing protects me from my own possibilities. This anxiety is unwelcome but disclosive; it reveals the groundlessness of choice that everyday absorption keeps hidden.

Moods are not mere inner feelings added on top of a neutral world; they are ways the world as a whole is disclosed. In anxiety, things lose their familiar significance and the world stands forth as strange. A mood is an attunement that opens a world in a particular light, and so it is, the phenomenologist claims, a mode of understanding rather than a private coloring.

If altruism is real, its existence is not thereby explained. One can grant that people sometimes act for others' sake and still ask how such motivation is possible, what in the structure of agency or of the self makes it intelligible. The reductive move of psychological egoism, whatever its failings, was at least an attempt at explanation, and its rejection leaves the explanatory task open.

Why be moral at all? If the question asks for a self-interested reason, it may have no satisfying answer, since morality sometimes requires sacrifice. But the question may be confused. To ask for a non-moral reason to be moral is to ask morality to justify itself at the bar of self-interest, and a morality that could be so justified would not be morality but prudence in disguise.

subtopic: the limits of language and the unsayable
sentence: If our concepts are the lenses through which anything appears, then a reality that fit none of our concepts would be, for us, no reality at all, since we could form no thought of it. This suggests the unsayable is not a hidden region we are barred from but the shadow cast by the very idea of a thought that no thinking could think.

Is religious belief something reason can assess, or does it answer to a different standard? Evidentialism holds that one ought to believe only in proportion to the evidence, and that faith asserted beyond the evidence is a violation of intellectual duty. On this view, religious belief stands or falls with the arguments, and to believe without them is to believe badly.

Virtue ethics handles the moral significance of emotion better than its rivals. A person who does the right thing while seething with resentment is, for virtue ethics, falling short, because virtue includes feeling rightly, not merely acting rightly. The fully virtuous agent acts from settled inclination, not from a struggle against contrary desire, and this fit between feeling and action is itself a moral achievement.

subtopic: the self and the unity of consciousness
sentence: Perhaps the self is best understood as a center of perspective rather than a substance. To be a self is to be the point from which a world is laid out, the locus of a take on things. Such a center need not be an extra item over and above the experiences; it may be a structural feature of how experience is organized, a vanishing point implied by the scene.

subtopic: determinism, chance, and the open future
sentence: The open future is often pictured as a branching tree: the past a single trunk, the future a spread of possibilities not yet narrowed to one. But if the future is genuinely open, it is unclear what makes statements about it true or false now. Either future contingents lack a present truth-value, or there is a fact about which branch will be actual, and the openness is only epistemic.

subtopic: logic and the foundations of inference
sentence: Dialetheism holds that some contradictions are true, that there are statements both true and false, and proposes a paraconsistent logic in which a contradiction does not entail everything. The view is heterodox, defended chiefly to handle the semantic paradoxes. Whether one can rationally accept a true contradiction, or whether the very idea undermines assertion, is fiercely contested.

If the deprivation account is right, then an immortal life would be invulnerable to the harm of death, since nothing would be deprived. But many argue that immortality would itself be a harm, that an endless life would exhaust all projects and decay into boredom. If so, death is bad and yet its absence would also be bad, and the good is a finite life of the right length.

Some respond that induction is constitutive of rationality itself: to be rational just is, in part, to weigh evidence inductively. On this view asking whether induction is rational is like asking whether the rules of a game are permitted by the game. The move is attractive but risks making 'rational' a label we award to our own habits.

Bentham reframed the question of animal status with a single line of thought: the question is not whether they can reason or talk but whether they can suffer. If sentience is the ground of moral considerability, then the capacity for suffering, widely shared among animals, brings them within the circle of moral concern, regardless of their intellectual powers.

subtopic: political authority and the social contract
sentence: Why should anyone obey the state? Its commands are backed by force, but force alone confers power, not authority, and authority is the right to be obeyed. The social contract tradition answers that authority derives from the consent of the governed: legitimate political power is power the governed have, in some sense, agreed to. The difficulty is to make sense of an agreement almost no one has explicitly given.

Nominalism denies that abstract mathematical objects exist and tries to make sense of mathematics without them. One strategy reconstrues mathematical statements as claims about what is possible, or about concrete inscriptions, or as useful fictions. The success of such reconstruals is contested, and the worry is that mathematics, indispensable to science, may not survive being stripped of its objects.

subtopic: political authority and the social contract
sentence: If consent grounds authority, anarchism follows for those who have not consented. The philosophical anarchist concludes that no state is legitimate, since genuine consent is absent, while granting that some states are better than others. Authority, on this view, is a moral relation almost never instantiated, and obedience to law, when justified, is justified by something other than the law's authority.

Modal realism takes possible worlds with full seriousness: they are concrete universes, as real as ours, spatiotemporally and causally isolated from each other. This gives a clean reduction of modality, since necessity becomes truth across a domain of existing things. The cost is an extravagant ontology, an infinity of cosmoses, accepted for the sake of theoretical economy in analysis.

The badness of death may depend on the life cut short. The death of a young person with rich possibilities deprives more than the death of someone very old whose central goods have been realized. This graduated picture matches common feeling, but it implies that the badness of death is not a constant, and that the same event differs in harm by who it befalls and when.

Camus posed the absurd as the confrontation between our demand for meaning and a universe that returns only silence. His response was neither resignation nor a leap to faith but lucid revolt: to live fully in awareness of the absurd without pretending it away. Whether this is a solution or a refusal to be consoled is part of what the absurd, by its nature, leaves open.

The fact that helping another brings the helper satisfaction does not show the helping was selfish. The satisfaction may be a consequence of caring about the other, not the aim of the action. Psychological egoism confuses the by-product of a desire with its object, and once that confusion is exposed, the apparent inevitability of self-interest as the universal motive dissolves.

Regularity theories hold that causation is instantiation of a law-like generalization: c causes e when c and e fall under a regularity. This honors Hume but struggles with the asymmetry of cause and effect, since regularities run both ways, and with distinguishing genuine laws from accidental uniformities that happen to hold without supporting causal claims.

Teleological theories add a normative element: a state means cat if its biological function is to be triggered by cats, even if it sometimes misfires. Misrepresentation becomes malfunction. The difficulty is fixing the function determinately. Was the detector selected to indicate cats, or small moving prey, or warm furry objects? Indeterminacy of function threatens to leave content indeterminate.

A reductionist about persons holds that the persistence of a person just consists in the holding of certain more particular facts, describable without presupposing identity. This is liberating, since it removes the demand for a deep further fact, but it is also unsettling, because it implies that the boundary of the self is conventional, and that the unity of a life is something we impose rather than find.

Resemblance nominalism dispenses with universals and explains shared character by resemblance among particulars: red things form a class because each resembles the others. The objection is that resemblance is itself a repeatable feature, a universal in disguise, and that the theory cannot, without circularity, say what makes the right resemblances the relevant ones.

Suppose a teleporter scans and destroys your body, then assembles an exact replica elsewhere. Did you travel, or did you die while a duplicate began a new life? The case is troubling because every fact about the replica is settled, yet the question of whether it is you appears to remain open. That suggests our concept of identity carries an assumption it cannot cash out.

No interpreter approaches a text empty-handed. We bring expectations, a fore-understanding shaped by our situation and tradition, and these prejudgments are the condition of understanding anything at all, not merely a distortion to be eliminated. The hermeneutic task is not to discard one's preconceptions but to bring them into play and let the text confirm or correct them.

The threat of cosmic insignificance presses that against the scale of the universe and the eons, nothing a person does could matter. But significance is not obviously a matter of scale. A kindness is not made worthless by the size of the galaxy, and the demand that meaning be visible from the standpoint of the cosmos may be a demand we have no reason to accept.

Humeans hold that reason alone cannot motivate; every action requires a desire, and reason only serves the desires we already have. Kantians hold that reason can be practical in its own right, that recognizing a duty can move us without a prior desire. The dispute concerns nothing less than whether morality can grip an agent who lacks the relevant inclinations.

subtopic: determinism, chance, and the open future
sentence: Even in a fully deterministic world, there is a sense in which the future is open to the deliberating agent: it is not yet decided by her, and her deliberation will help decide it. The openness that matters for action may be epistemic and deliberative rather than metaphysical, the openness of a question one is in the process of answering.

Rule utilitarianism shifts the calculation from acts to rules: choose the set of rules whose general adoption maximizes welfare, then act on them. This blunts the worry that the theory licenses individual atrocities. But critics charge that a rule utilitarian who would not break a welfare-maximizing rule even when breaking it would do more good has stopped maximizing welfare, and a rule utilitarian who would break it has collapsed back into act utilitarianism.

The explanatory gap is sometimes blamed on the limits of human cognition rather than on reality itself. Perhaps a mind built differently could see why neural firing must feel like something. On this view the hard problem is real but soluble in principle, just not by us. That is a humbling thought, yet it still concedes that present concepts leave the connection between brain and experience genuinely opaque.

When I see a tomato, do I see the tomato itself or only a private appearance from which I infer the tomato? The sense-datum theory holds that the immediate object of perception is a mind-dependent appearance, and that physical objects are known only mediately. This explains illusion and hallucination neatly but threatens to seal the mind off behind a veil of its own appearances.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: Notice that the bystander's options are themselves a moral artifact: the scenario presents two choices and forbids a third. Real cases rarely come so cleanly framed. Part of moral skill is recognizing that the way a situation is described already encodes assumptions about what is up to the agent, and the trolley problem, by fixing the frame, brackets that skill in order to examine a narrower one.

Understanding a work from a distant age requires bridging a gulf of assumptions. The interpreter and the text each stand within a horizon, a range of what can be seen from a given vantage. Understanding occurs, on one influential account, as a fusion of horizons, in which the interpreter's outlook is widened by genuine engagement with the strangeness of the other.

Application is internal to understanding, on the hermeneutic account, not a step that follows it. To understand a law, a moral teaching, or a text addressed to life is already to work out what it asks of one's own situation. Understanding, on this view, is never a purely contemplative grasp of a fixed content; it is always also a working-out of significance for the interpreter.

One response holds that experience is fundamental, on a par with mass or charge, rather than derived from anything more basic. This dissolves the demand for a reductive explanation by denying that one is owed. But it purchases that relief at a cost: it must then explain how fundamental experiential properties combine into the unified consciousness of a single mind, a difficulty no less severe than the one it was meant to escape.

The argument from queerness presses that objective moral facts would have to be intrinsically motivating and intrinsically authoritative, unlike any natural fact, and that a faculty to detect them would be unlike any other faculty. The realist can answer either by denying that moral facts have these queer features or by arguing that their queerness is no worse than that of mathematical or modal facts we already accept.

Notice the self-locating peculiarity of the vat scenario: it is designed so that its truth would leave no trace in your experience. A hypothesis with that feature can never be confirmed or disconfirmed by you. One might conclude it is therefore not a genuine alternative at all, since alternatives must in principle be distinguishable. The skeptic will say genuineness does not require detectability, and the debate descends to that point.

subtopic: the categorical imperative and moral law
sentence: Some maxims can be conceived as universal without contradiction yet cannot be willed as universal. A maxim of never helping others in need could obtain as a universal law, but a rational agent cannot will it, since she may herself need help and would thereby will away aid she might require. This contradiction in the will grounds the imperfect duty of beneficence.

The error theory accepts that moral language aims to describe objective facts but holds that there are none, so all positive moral claims are false. This is a bold and unsettling view: it implies that 'torture is wrong' and 'torture is permissible' are both untrue, the way claims about phlogiston are. Its motivation is that objective prescriptivity, a feature built into moral concepts, is too queer to exist.

subtopic: the categorical imperative and moral law
sentence: The conflict-of-duties objection asks what the categorical imperative says when two duties collide, since an unconditional command seems unable to yield. Kant holds that there cannot be a genuine conflict of obligations, only of grounds of obligation, with the stronger ground determining the duty. Whether this resolves hard cases or merely relabels them is a question Kantians continue to debate.

Consciousness, the phenomenologist observes, is always consciousness of something; it is never a bare inner glow but always reaches toward an object. This intentionality is not a contingent fact but the very structure of mental life. To describe an experience is therefore to describe both the act and what it presents, and the two cannot be prised apart without distortion.

Scientific realism holds that our best theories are approximately true and that the unobservable entities they posit, electrons, fields, genes, really exist. The chief argument is that the predictive success of these theories would be a miracle if they were not at least roughly latching onto how the world is. Anti-realists must explain success some other way, or accept the miracle.

One reply concedes that induction cannot be justified in advance but insists it can be vindicated: if any method will work, induction will, since it is self-correcting in the long run. Yet 'the long run' is itself a future-directed notion, and the claim that induction will work is the very thing in question. The vindication seems to smuggle in what it set out to provide.

Class nominalism identifies a property with the class of its instances: to be red is to belong to the class of red things. But classes are extensional, so coextensive properties would be identical, and if every creature with a heart had a kidney, having a heart would be the same property as having a kidney, which is false.

The minimalist holds that we grasp truth fully through the schema 'the proposition that p is true if and only if p,' and that nothing deeper underlies it. Every instance of the schema is trivial, yet together they fix the concept. Critics doubt that a concept can be exhausted by an open-ended list of trivialities, and suspect that the schema presupposes rather than explains what truth is.

The coherence theory holds that truth is membership in a maximally coherent system of beliefs. It answers the question of access, since coherence is something we can assess from within. But it seems to make truth too cheap: a beautifully coherent fiction would count as true, and there is no evident reason why exactly one maximal system should be coherent rather than many incompatible ones.

Beauty and the sublime were long distinguished. Beauty pleases through harmony, proportion, and a sense of fit; the sublime overwhelms, in the vast and the formless, mingling a kind of terror with exaltation. The sublime suggests that aesthetic value is not a single quality but a family, and that some of its members trade comfort for the thrill of being exceeded.

Knowledge has long been analyzed as justified true belief: you know that p if p is true, you believe it, and your belief is justified. The analysis is attractive because each condition seems necessary. Gettier showed it is not sufficient: one can have a justified true belief that is true by luck, and luck is exactly what knowledge excludes.

A familiar objection charges that virtue ethics gives no action guidance: telling an agent to do what the virtuous person would do is unhelpful if she does not know what that is. The reply is that all theories ultimately rely on judgment, and that the virtuous person's perception of the salient features of a situation is itself a form of guidance, just not an algorithmic one.

The problem of evil need not assume theism is false to be philosophically serious. It can be read as an internal challenge: given the concept of a perfect being, can the facts of suffering be accommodated coherently? Even an atheist can find the problem instructive, for it probes how the notions of power, knowledge, and goodness interact, and how far a value can excuse a cost.

The cosmological argument reasons from the existence of contingent things to a necessary being that grounds them. Everything that might not have existed depends for its existence on something else; the chain of dependence cannot regress without end or circle back; so there must be something that exists not by depending on another but by its own nature. Whether such a being deserves the name God is a further question.

subtopic: the trolley problem and moral intuition
sentence: A consequentialist sees no real difference: five deaths are worse than one, so both diverting and pushing are required. The widespread reluctance to push is then a moral error, perhaps a useful instinct that misfires in artificial cases. The opponent replies that an instinct this stable and this widely shared is data, not noise, and a theory that overrides it owes us an account of why our intuitions are so reliably wrong.

The recalcitrant emotion poses a problem for any view that ties emotion too tightly to judgment. One can fear the spider while judging, on full reflection, that it is harmless. The fear persists against the judgment. This shows that whatever evaluative element an emotion carries, it is not simply a belief, since beliefs do not survive their owner's sincere rejection in this way.

Tolerance is sometimes offered as the lesson of relativism, but the inference is self-defeating. If relativism holds that no value is objectively binding, then tolerance is not objectively binding either, and a culture that rejects tolerance cannot be faulted. Relativism cannot ground a universal duty of tolerance without abandoning the relativism that was supposed to recommend it.

Source incompatibilism locates the problem not in the absence of alternatives but in the agent's not being the ultimate source of the action.
